claim: The spindle position checkpoint (SPOC) is a spindle pole body (SPB) associated surveillance mechanism that halts mitotic exit upon spindle mis-orientation.
source: The spindle position checkpoint (SPOC) is a spindle pole body (SPB, equivalent of mammalian centrosome) associated surveillance mechanism that halts mitotic exit upon spindle mis-orientation.
evidence: This is a definitional statement from the abstract that establishes the function of SPOC.

claim: Bfa1 binds to the scaffold-protein Nud1.
source: We show that Bfa1 binds to the scaffold-protein Nud1 and the γ-tubulin receptor Spc72.
evidence: Supported by FRET microscopy data shown in Figure 1A and in vitro binding assays.

claim: Bfa1 binds to the γ-tubulin receptor Spc72.
source: We show that Bfa1 binds to the scaffold-protein Nud1 and the γ-tubulin receptor Spc72.
evidence: Supported by FRET microscopy data shown in Figure 1A and in vitro binding assays shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Spindle misalignment specifically disrupts Bfa1-Spc72 interaction.
source: Spindle misalignment specifically disrupts Bfa1-Spc72 interaction by a mechanism that requires the 14-3-3-family protein Bmh1 and the MARK/PAR-kinase Kin4.
evidence: Supported by FRET data shown in Figure 3F demonstrating loss of FRET between Bfa1 and Spc72 upon spindle misalignment.

claim: Disruption of Bfa1-Spc72 interaction requires the 14-3-3-family protein Bmh1.
source: Spindle misalignment specifically disrupts Bfa1-Spc72 interaction by a mechanism that requires the 14-3-3-family protein Bmh1 and the MARK/PAR-kinase Kin4.
evidence: Supported by FRET data in Figure 3C showing that deletion of BMH1 prevents the loss of Bfa1-Spc72 FRET upon KIN4 overexpression.

claim: Disruption of Bfa1-Spc72 interaction requires the MARK/PAR-kinase Kin4.
source: Spindle misalignment specifically disrupts Bfa1-Spc72 interaction by a mechanism that requires the 14-3-3-family protein Bmh1 and the MARK/PAR-kinase Kin4.
evidence: Supported by FRET data in Figure 3G and H showing that deletion of KIN4 prevents loss of Bfa1-Spc72 FRET upon spindle misalignment.

claim: Dissociation of Bfa1 from Spc72 prevents the inhibitory phosphorylation of Bfa1 by the polo-like kinase Cdc5.
source: Dissociation of Bfa1 from Spc72 prevents the inhibitory phosphorylation of Bfa1 by the polo-like kinase Cdc5.
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 7C showing that forced binding of Bfa1 to Spc72 (via Spc72-GBP) results in increased Cdc5-dependent phosphorylation of Bfa1.

claim: Spc72 is a regulatory hub that coordinates the activity of Kin4 and Cdc5 towards Bfa1.
source: We propose Spc72 as a regulatory hub that coordinates the activity of Kin4 and Cdc5 towards Bfa1.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on data showing that both Kin4 and Cdc5 require Spc72 to phosphorylate Bfa1.

claim: A mitotic-exit-promoting dominant signal triggered upon elongation of the spindle into the bud overrides the SPOC in spc72∆ cells.
source: In addition, analysis of spc72∆ cells shows that a mitotic-exit-promoting dominant signal, which is triggered upon elongation of the spindle into the bud, overrides the SPOC.
evidence: Supported by time-lapse data in Figure 8D and E showing that in binucleated spc72∆ cells with two spindles, re-alignment of one spindle is sufficient to trigger mitotic exit in both nuclei.

claim: SPBs are embedded in the nuclear envelope throughout the cell cycle.
source: SPBs are embedded in the nuclear envelope throughout the cell cycle and are composed of three distinct layers (inner, central and outer plaques) that are named according to their position with respect to the nuclear envelope (Jaspersen and Winey, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jaspersen and Winey, 2004.

claim: SPBs are composed of three distinct layers: inner, central and outer plaques.
source: SPBs are embedded in the nuclear envelope throughout the cell cycle and are composed of three distinct layers (inner, central and outer plaques) that are named according to their position with respect to the nuclear envelope (Jaspersen and Winey, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jaspersen and Winey, 2004.

claim: SPOC and MEN proteins associate with the cytoplasmic side (outer plaque) of the SPBs.
source: SPOC and MEN proteins associate with the cytoplasmic side (outer plaque) of the SPBs, where cytoplasmic microtubules are nucleated.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SPB structure and protein localization.

claim: Spc72 anchors the γ-tubulin small complexes that nucleate cytoplasmic microtubules.
source: Within this outer plaque, the transforming acidic coiled coil (TACC) family protein Spc72 (the yeast homolog of CDK5RAP2) anchors the γ-tubulin small complexes that nucleate cytoplasmic microtubules (Knop and Schiebel, 1998; Lin et al., 2015; Usui et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Knop and Schiebel, 1998; Lin et al., 2015; Usui et al., 2003.

claim: Nud1 links Spc72 to the central layer of the SPB through Cnm67.
source: Nud1 (the yeast homolog of Centriolin) links Spc72 to the central layer of the SPB through Cnm67 - another SPB core protein (Brachat et al., 1998; Elliott et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brachat et al., 1998; Elliott et al., 1999.

claim: Nud1 serves as a scaffold for the recruitment and activation of MEN kinases.
source: Nud1 also serves as a scaffold for the recruitment and activation of MEN kinases (Gruneberg et al., 2000; Rock and Amon, 2011; Rock et al., 2013; Valerio-Santiago and Monje-Casas, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gruneberg et al., 2000; Rock and Amon, 2011; Rock et al., 2013; Valerio-Santiago and Monje-Casas, 2011.

claim: The key element of SPOC is a GTPase activating protein (GAP) complex composed of the GAP Bub2 and its binding partner Bfa1.
source: The key element of SPOC is a GTPase activating protein (GAP) complex composed of the GAP Bub2 and its binding partner Bfa1 (Bardin et al., 2000; Pereira et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bardin et al., 2000; Pereira et al., 2000.

claim: The GAP-complex inhibits the GTPase Tem1.
source: The GAP-complex inhibits the GTPase Tem1, whose activation would otherwise trigger the MEN (Bardin et al., 2000; Geymonat et al., 2002; 2003; Hu et al., 2001; Pereira et al., 2000; Scarfone and Piatti, 2015; Wang et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Loss of SPOC function in cells with misaligned spindles leads to multi-nucleation and anucleation.
source: Loss of SPOC function in cells with misaligned spindles leads to multi-nucleation and anucleation, as cells undergo mitotic exit and cytokinesis irrespective of whether one nucleus has migrated into the daughter cell or not.
evidence: This is established knowledge about SPOC function.

claim: The Bfa1-Bub2 complex localizes interdependently at the SPB outer plaque throughout the cell cycle.
source: The two components of the bi-partite Bfa1-Bub2 GAP complex localize interdependently at the SPB outer plaque throughout the cell cycle (Lee et al., 2001; Pereira et al., 2000; 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2001; Pereira et al., 2000; 2001.

claim: During normal spindle alignment, the Bfa1-Bub2 complex is unequally distributed between the two SPBs, to predominantly associate with the SPB that is directed towards the daughter cell (dSPB).
source: During normal spindle alignment, the Bfa1-Bub2 complex is unequally distributed between the two SPBs, to predominantly associate with the SPB that is directed towards the daughter cell (dSPB) (asymmetric localization) (Fraschini et al., 2006; Pereira et al., 2000; 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fraschini et al., 2006; Pereira et al., 2000; 2001.

claim: As long as the spindle is correctly positioned, Bfa1-Bub2 remains stably bound to the dSPB.
source: As long as the spindle is correctly positioned, Bfa1-Bub2 remains stably bound to the dSPB (Caydasi and Pereira, 2009; Monje-Casas and Amon, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Caydasi and Pereira, 2009; Monje-Casas and Amon, 2009.

claim: As soon as the anaphase spindle moves into the daughter cell compartment, Bfa1 is inactivated by the conserved polo-like kinase Cdc5 that inhibits Bfa1-Bub2 GAP activity.
source: As soon as the anaphase spindle moves into the daughter cell compartment, Bfa1 is inactivated by the conserved polo-like kinase Cdc5 that inhibits Bfa1-Bub2 GAP activity (Geymonat et al., 2002; 2003; Hu and Elledge, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Geymonat et al., 2002; 2003; Hu and Elledge, 2002.

claim: Upon spindle misalignment, the MARK/PAR family kinase Kin4 is recruited to the Spc72 component of both SPBs.
source: Upon spindle misalignment, the MARK/PAR family kinase Kin4 is recruited to the Spc72 component of both SPBs (D'Aquino et al., 2005; Maekawa et al., 2007; Pereira and Schiebel, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to D'Aquino et al., 2005; Maekawa et al., 2007; Pereira and Schiebel, 2005.

claim: Phosphorylation of Bfa1 by Kin4 at SPBs converts the asymmetric and stable SPB localization of Bfa1-Bub2 into a symmetric and dynamic association.
source: Phosphorylation of Bfa1 by Kin4 at SPBs converts the asymmetric and stable SPB localization of Bfa1-Bub2 into a symmetric (same amount on each SPB) and dynamic association (Caydasi and Pereira, 2009; Monje-Casas and Amon, 2009; Pereira et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Caydasi and Pereira, 2009; Monje-Casas and Amon, 2009; Pereira et al., 2000.

claim: Kin4 reduces the levels of SPB-bound Bfa1.
source: Kin4 also reduces the levels of SPB-bound Bfa1 (Caydasi and Pereira, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Caydasi and Pereira, 2009.

claim: Changes in Bfa1-Bub2 SPB localization are essential for SPOC function and require binding of the 14-3-3 family protein Bmh1 to Bfa1 previously phosphorylated by Kin4 kinase.
source: These drastic changes in Bfa1-Bub2 SPB localization are essential for SPOC function and require binding of the 14-3-3 family protein Bmh1 to Bfa1 previously phosphorylated by Kin4 kinase (Caydasi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Caydasi et al., 2014.

claim: Acceptor photobleaching FRET monitors the increase in donor fluorescence upon photobleaching of the acceptor.
source: In contrast to the conventional FRET detection, which is based on acceptor emission measurements (i.e., sensitized emission FRET), the acceptor photobleaching FRET monitors the increase in donor fluorescence upon photobleaching of the acceptor (i.e., donor de-quenching) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Llopis et al., 2000; Wouters and Bastiaens, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Llopis et al., 2000; Wouters and Bastiaens, 2001.

claim: The proportionate increase in the donor fluorescence intensity after photobleaching of the acceptor directly yields the apparent FRET efficiency.
source: The proportionate increase in the donor fluorescence intensity after photobleaching of the acceptor directly yields the apparent FRET efficiency (EFRET) (Karpova et al., 2003; Kentner and Sourjik, 2009), which is further corrected for the unspecific signal observed in the donor-only sample (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Karpova et al., 2003; Kentner and Sourjik, 2009.

claim: The topology of the core SPB proteins including Spc42, Cnm67 and Spc110 has been previously defined by sensitized emission FRET.
source: The topology of the core SPB proteins including Spc42, Cnm67 and Spc110 has been previously defined by sensitized emission FRET (Muller et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Muller et al., 2005.

claim: Acceptor photobleaching FRET technique yielded a positive FRET interaction between Spc42-mTUR and Cnm67-EYFP.
source: In agreement with published data (Muller et al., 2005), the acceptor photobleaching FRET technique yielded a positive FRET interaction between Spc42-mTUR and Cnm67-EYFP (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, 14% mean FRET efficiency in the donor-acceptor pair), while no FRET was detected for the Spc110-mTUR and Cnm67-EYFP pair (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and is consistent with published data from Muller et al., 2005.

claim: No FRET was detected for the Spc110-mTUR and Cnm67-EYFP pair.
source: In agreement with published data (Muller et al., 2005), the acceptor photobleaching FRET technique yielded a positive FRET interaction between Spc42-mTUR and Cnm67-EYFP (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, 14% mean FRET efficiency in the donor-acceptor pair), while no FRET was detected for the Spc110-mTUR and Cnm67-EYFP pair (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and is consistent with published data from Muller et al., 2005.

claim: Bfa1-EYFP-mTUR yielded a FRET value of 26% at SPBs.
source: Bfa1-EYFP-mTUR yielded a FRET value of 26% at SPBs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), to define the maximum value that can be measured for this particular donor-acceptor pair (mTUR-EYFP).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: No FRET was detected in the cytoplasm using the chimeric Bfa1-mTUR-YFP tandem pair.
source: We could however detect no FRET in the cytoplasm using the chimeric Bfa1-mTUR-YFP tandem pair (data not shown), indicating that the concentration of Bfa1 in the cytoplasm sits below our FRET detection limit.
evidence: This is stated in the text but data is not shown.

claim: Bfa1-Bub2 localize to the outer plaque.
source: Immuno-electron microscopy has established that Bfa1-Bub2 localize to the outer plaque (Pereira et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pereira et al., 2000.

claim: C-terminal tagging of Nud1, Spc72 and Cnm67 with fluorescent proteins did not affect their functionality in microtubule organization.
source: C-terminal tagging of Nud1, Spc72 and Cnm67 with fluorescent proteins did not affect their functionality in microtubule organization, as no defect in nuclear migration and positioning was observed in strains encoding tagged proteins (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B) (Grava et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B and a citation to Grava et al., 2006.

claim: Deletion of KAR9 causes frequent spindle misalignment at non-permissive temperatures.
source: Deletion of KAR9 causes frequent spindle misalignment at non-permissive temperatures (Miller and Rose, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Miller and Rose, 1998.

claim: In the absence of SPOC function, kar9Δ cultures accumulate multi-nucleated or anucleated cells.
source: In the absence of SPOC function, kar9Δ cultures accumulate multi-nucleated or anucleated cells because cells exit mitosis without having segregated chromosomes into the daughter cell compartment (Bardin et al., 2000; Pereira et al., 2000) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C and citations to Bardin et al., 2000; Pereira et al., 2000.

claim: kar9∆ cells carrying C-terminally tagged BUB2 or N-terminally tagged BFA1 were SPOC deficient.
source: kar9∆ cells carrying C-terminally tagged BUB2 or N-terminally tagged BFA1 were SPOC deficient (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Cells harboring C-terminal fusions of BFA1, NUD1 or SPC72 and N-terminal fusions of BUB2 with mTUR or EYFP retained SPOC function.
source: Cells harboring C-terminal fusions of BFA1, NUD1 or SPC72 and N-terminal fusions of BUB2 with mTUR or EYFP retained SPOC function (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C and 3D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C and 3D.

claim: Pairing Bfa1-EYFP with Nud1-mTUR yielded a FRET signal.
source: Pairing Bfa1-EYFP with Nud1-mTUR or Spc72-mTUR yielded a FRET signal, whereas no FRET was detected between Bfa1-EYFP and Cnm67-mTUR (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Pairing Bfa1-EYFP with Spc72-mTUR yielded a FRET signal.
source: Pairing Bfa1-EYFP with Nud1-mTUR or Spc72-mTUR yielded a FRET signal, whereas no FRET was detected between Bfa1-EYFP and Cnm67-mTUR (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: No FRET was detected between Bfa1-EYFP and Cnm67-mTUR.
source: Pairing Bfa1-EYFP with Nud1-mTUR or Spc72-mTUR yielded a FRET signal, whereas no FRET was detected between Bfa1-EYFP and Cnm67-mTUR (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Similar FRET efficiencies were measured in metaphase- and anaphase-arrested cells for Bfa1-Nud1 and Bfa1-Spc72 pairs.
source: Similar FRET efficiencies were measured in metaphase- and anaphase-arrested cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: mTUR-Bub2 did not display any FRET when paired with Nud1-EYFP or Spc72-EYFP.
source: Unlike Bfa1, mTUR-Bub2 did not display any FRET when paired with Nud1-EYFP or Spc72-EYFP (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The mTUR-Bub2 and Bfa1-EYFP combination generated a FRET signal at SPBs.
source: Importantly, the mTUR-Bub2 and Bfa1-EYFP combination generated a FRET signal at SPBs (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The C-terminus of Bfa1 resides in close proximity to the C-termini of both Nud1 and Spc72 at SPBs.
source: These data show that the C-terminus of Bfa1 resides in close proximity to the C-termini of both Nud1 and Spc72 at SPBs.
evidence: This is inferred from the FRET data showing positive FRET between C-terminally tagged Bfa1 and C-terminally tagged Nud1 and Spc72.

claim: The C-terminus of Bfa1 is positioned in close proximity to the N-terminus of Bub2.
source: The C-terminus of Bfa1 is also positioned in close proximity to the N-terminus of Bub2, in support of their binding to SPBs as a protein complex (Pereira et al., 2000).
evidence: This is inferred from the FRET data and supported by a citation to Pereira et al., 2000.

claim: The levels of FRET between Bfa1-Nud1 were similar at the mSPB and dSPB.
source: The levels of FRET between Bfa1-Nud1 or Bfa1-Spc72 were similar at the mSPB and dSPB (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: The levels of FRET between Bfa1-Spc72 were similar at the mSPB and dSPB.
source: The levels of FRET between Bfa1-Nud1 or Bfa1-Spc72 were similar at the mSPB and dSPB (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Bfa1 is in close proximity with Nud1 and Spc72 on both SPBs.
source: This indicates that Bfa1 is in close proximity with Nud1 and Spc72 on both SPBs.
evidence: This is inferred from the FRET data showing similar FRET efficiencies at both SPBs.

claim: Asymmetric SPB localization of Bfa1 cannot be dictated by the differential association of Bfa1 with Spc72 or Nud1.
source: Thus, asymmetric SPB localization of Bfa1 cannot be dictated by the differential association of Bfa1 with Spc72 or Nud1.
evidence: This is inferred from the FRET data showing similar FRET efficiencies at both SPBs despite asymmetric Bfa1 localization.

claim: Changes in the donor:acceptor ratio do not affect FRET measurements in our experimental system.
source: The values of FRET efficiency did not correlate with the signal intensity of the acceptor. Thus, changes in the donor:acceptor ratio do not affect FRET measurements in our experimental system.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2E and F showing no correlation between FRET efficiency and acceptor fluorescence intensity.

claim: Overexpression of KIN4 activates the SPOC to arrest cells in late anaphase, even when the spindle is correctly aligned.
source: Overexpression of KIN4 activates the SPOC to arrest cells in late anaphase, even when the spindle is correctly aligned (D'Aquino et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to D'Aquino et al., 2005.

claim: FRET between Bfa1 and Nud1 was maintained in KIN4 overexpressing cells.
source: FRET between Bfa1 and Nud1 was maintained in KIN4 overexpressing cells (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The FRET between Bfa1-Spc72 pair disappeared upon KIN4 overexpression.
source: In contrast, the FRET between Bfa1-Spc72 pair disappeared upon KIN4 overexpression (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Kin4 activity specifically disturbs the interaction between Bfa1 and Spc72 but not that between Bfa1 and Nud1.
source: Thus, Kin4 activity specifically disturbs the interaction between Bfa1 and Spc72 but not that between Bfa1 and Nud1.
evidence: This is inferred from the FRET data showing loss of Bfa1-Spc72 FRET but maintenance of Bfa1-Nud1 FRET upon KIN4 overexpression.

claim: Binding of Bmh1 to Kin4-phosphorylated Bfa1 abolishes the stable association of Bfa1 with SPBs.
source: We previously described how binding of Bmh1 to Kin4-phosphorylated Bfa1 abolishes the stable association of Bfa1 with SPBs (Caydasi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Caydasi et al., 2014.

claim: In cells lacking BMH1, Bfa1 remains asymmetrically and stably associated with SPBs, even when Kin4 phosphorylates Bfa1.
source: In cells lacking BMH1, Bfa1 remains asymmetrically and stably associated with SPBs, even when Kin4 phosphorylates Bfa1 (Caydasi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Caydasi et al., 2014.

claim: Kin4 overexpression in the presence of BMH1 greatly decreased the FRET efficiency of the Bfa1-Spc72 pair.
source: Kin4 overexpression in the presence of BMH1 greatly decreased the FRET efficiency of the Bfa1-Spc72 pair (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Kin4 overexpression did not decrease the FRET efficiency of the Bfa1-Spc72 pair in bmh1∆ cells.
source: This was not the case in bmh1∆ cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Deletion of BMH1 did not influence the FRET efficiency of Nud1–Bfa1 pair.
source: Deletion of BMH1 did not influence the FRET efficiency of Nud1–Bfa1 pair (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Spindle position had no impact upon FRET between Bfa1 and Nud1.
source: Spindle position had no impact upon FRET between Bfa1 and Nud1 (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Spindle misalignment reduced the FRET efficiency of the Bfa1-Spc72 pair to the level seen in the donor-only control.
source: In contrast, spindle misalignment reduced the FRET efficiency of the Bfa1-Spc72 pair to the level seen in the donor-only control (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: In the absence of KIN4, the FRET between Bfa1 and Spc72 persisted irrespective of spindle position.
source: In the absence of KIN4, however, the FRET between Bfa1 and Spc72 persisted irrespective of spindle position (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3G and H.

claim: Upon spindle misalignment, Kin4, with the assistance of Bmh1, rearranges Bfa1 molecules on the SPB by specifically influencing the Bfa1-Spc72 interaction.
source: Together, these data show that, upon spindle misalignment, Kin4, with the assistance of Bmh1, rearranges Bfa1 molecules on the SPB by specifically influencing the Bfa1-Spc72 interaction.
evidence: This is inferred from the FRET data showing that Kin4 and Bmh1 are required for loss of Bfa1-Spc72 FRET upon spindle misalignment.

claim: Bfa1 associated with Nud1 at SPBs of spc72∆ cells regardless of spindle orientation.
source: FRET analysis showed that Bfa1 associated with Nud1 at SPBs of spc72∆ cells regardless of spindle orientation (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: SPB-bound Bfa1 levels were not reduced in spc72∆ cells.
source: Interestingly, SPB-bound Bfa1 levels were not reduced in spc72∆ cells (Figure 4D), arguing against the model where there are two pools of Bfa1 that separately bind Spc72 and Nud1.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Bfa1-GFP failed to recover at SPBs in cells with normally aligned anaphase spindles in the presence of SPC72.
source: After photobleaching, Bfa1-GFP failed to recover at SPBs in cells with normally aligned anaphase spindles in the presence of SPC72 (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Cells lacking SPC72 recruited Bfa1-GFP stably to the dSPB when the anaphase spindle was correctly aligned.
source: Cells lacking SPC72 also recruited Bfa1-GFP stably to the dSPB when the anaphase spindle was correctly aligned (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Bfa1 interaction with Nud1 is stable throughout anaphase when spindle is correctly aligned, independently of Spc72.
source: Thus, Bfa1 interaction with Nud1 is stable throughout anaphase when spindle is correctly aligned, independently of Spc72.
evidence: This is inferred from the FRAP data showing stable Bfa1 binding in both SPC72 and spc72∆ cells with correctly aligned spindles.

claim: In the presence of SPC72, Bfa1 was highly dynamic at both SPBs with a half recovery time of ~ 11 s during spindle misalignment.
source: Consistent with previous data, in the presence of SPC72, Bfa1 was highly dynamic at both SPBs with a half recovery time of ~ 11 s during spindle misalignment (Figure 4F and 4G) (Caydasi and Pereira, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 4F and 4G and a citation to Caydasi and Pereira, 2009.

claim: The half recovery time of Bfa1 was 6 times longer in spc72∆ cells than in SPC72 cells during spindle misalignment.
source: The half recovery time of Bfa1 was 6 times longer in spc72∆ cells than in SPC72 cells (Figure 4F and 4G).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 4F and 4G.

claim: Spc72 regulates the mode of Bfa1 association with Nud1 when the spindle is mis-positioned.
source: These data suggest that Spc72 regulates the mode of Bfa1 association with Nud1 when the spindle is mis-positioned.
evidence: This is inferred from the FRAP data showing different Bfa1 dynamics in SPC72 and spc72∆ cells with misaligned spindles.

claim: Bfa1 molecules simultaneously associate with Nud1 and Spc72.
source: Together, our data favor a model in which Bfa1 molecules simultaneously associate with Nud1 and Spc72 (Figure 4A, ii).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the data showing that Bfa1 binds to SPBs via Nud1 in the absence of Spc72.

claim: In cells with properly aligned spindles, Nud1 is sufficient to stably recruit Bfa1 to SPBs independently of Spc72.
source: In cells with properly aligned spindles, Nud1 is sufficient to stably recruit Bfa1 to SPBs independently of Spc72.
evidence: This is inferred from the FRAP data showing stable Bfa1 binding in spc72∆ cells with correctly aligned spindles.

claim: In cells with misaligned spindles, Spc72 becomes indispensable to regulate Bfa1 SPB binding dynamics.
source: However, in cells with misaligned spindles, Spc72 becomes indispensable to regulate Bfa1 SPB binding dynamics.
evidence: This is inferred from the FRAP data showing reduced Bfa1 dynamics in spc72∆ cells with misaligned spindles.

claim: Bfa1-SPB binding dynamics in spc72∆ cells during spindle misalignment were reminiscent of those seen in kin4∆ cells.
source: Bfa1-SPB binding dynamics in spc72∆ cells during spindle misalignment were reminiscent of those seen in kin4∆ cells (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This is supported by FRAP data shown in Figure 4F and G.

claim: Spc72 recruits Kin4 to SPBs.
source: This is consistent with previous reports that Spc72 recruits Kin4 to SPBs and that Kin4 SPB binding is necessary for its function in SPOC (D'Aquino et al., 2005; Maekawa et al., 2007; Pereira and Schiebel, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to D'Aquino et al., 2005; Maekawa et al., 2007; Pereira and Schiebel, 2005.

claim: Kin4 SPB binding is necessary for its function in SPOC.
source: This is consistent with previous reports that Spc72 recruits Kin4 to SPBs and that Kin4 SPB binding is necessary for its function in SPOC (D'Aquino et al., 2005; Maekawa et al., 2007; Pereira and Schiebel, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to D'Aquino et al., 2005; Maekawa et al., 2007; Pereira and Schiebel, 2005.

claim: Kin4 was not detected at SPBs in spc72∆ cells by fluorescence microscopy.
source: Indeed, we were unable to detect Kin4 at SPBs in spc72∆ cells by fluorescence microscopy (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Phospho-specific antibodies could not detect Bfa1 phosphorylation at S180 in spc72∆ cells.
source: Neither could phospho-specific antibodies detect Bfa1 phosphorylation at S180 (one of the two sites phosphorylated by Kin4) in spc72∆ cells (Maekawa et al., 2007) (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5C and a citation to Maekawa et al., 2007.

claim: Bfa1 failed to bind symmetrically to SPBs in spc72∆ cells upon spindle misalignment.
source: Furthermore, the failure of Bfa1 to bind symmetrically (with same levels) to SPBs in spc72∆ cells upon spindle misalignment was also reminiscent of the kin4∆ phenotype (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Kin4 is unable to phosphorylate Bfa1 and dislodge Bfa1 from SPBs in the absence of Spc72.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that Kin4 is unable to phosphorylate Bfa1 and dislodge Bfa1 from SPBs in the absence of Spc72.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing lack of Kin4 SPB localization, lack of Bfa1 phosphorylation at S180, and lack of symmetric Bfa1 localization in spc72∆ cells.

claim: The reduction of Bfa1-SPB binding dynamics in spc72∆ cells with misaligned spindles is likely to arise from a lack of Kin4 phosphorylation of Bfa1.
source: Thus, the reduction of Bfa1-SPB binding dynamics in spc72∆ cells with misaligned spindles is likely to arise from a lack of Kin4 phosphorylation of Bfa1.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that spc72∆ cells phenocopy kin4∆ cells in terms of Bfa1 dynamics.

claim: spc72∆ cells were able to sustain an anaphase arrest for the duration of the time-lapse movie (>60 min) upon spindle mis-orientation.
source: To our surprise, spc72∆ cells were able to sustain an anaphase arrest for the duration of the time-lapse movie (>60 min) upon spindle mis-orientation (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: spc72∆ cells exited mitosis 23 min after the onset of spindle elongation when their spindle elongated along the correct mother-daughter cell axis.
source: This delay did not arise from a general deficiency that would extend anaphase because cells exited mitosis 23 min after the onset of spindle elongation when their spindle elongated along the correct mother-daughter cell axis (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claim: Deletion of BFA1 was lethal in spc72∆ cells.
source: Furthermore, deletion of BFA1 was lethal in spc72∆ cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), indicating that these cells require SPOC function for survival.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: spc72∆ cells require SPOC function for survival.
source: Furthermore, deletion of BFA1 was lethal in spc72∆ cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), indicating that these cells require SPOC function for survival.
evidence: This is inferred from the lethality of bfa1∆ spc72∆ double mutant.

claim: Despite the loss of Bfa1 phosphorylation by Kin4, disruption of Bfa1-Spc72 interaction by means of SPC72 deletion did not compromise the ability of cells with misaligned spindles to engage SPOC arrest.
source: Thus, despite the loss of Bfa1 phosphorylation by Kin4, disruption of Bfa1-Spc72 interaction by means of SPC72 deletion did not compromise the ability of cells with misaligned spindles to engage SPOC arrest.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that spc72∆ cells are SPOC proficient despite lack of Kin4 phosphorylation of Bfa1.

claim: Bfa1 phosphorylation by Kin4 is required to prevent Cdc5 phosphorylation of Bfa1 in wild type cells.
source: In wild type cells, Bfa1 phosphorylation by Kin4 is required to prevent Cdc5 phosphorylation of Bfa1, which would otherwise inhibit Bfa1-Bub2 GAP activity and so promote mitotic exit (D'Aquino et al., 2005; Geymonat et al., 2003; Pereira and Schiebel, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to D'Aquino et al., 2005; Geymonat et al., 2003; Pereira and Schiebel, 2005.

claim: Bfa1 becomes hyper-phosphorylated by Cdc5 in kin4∆ cells.
source: Bfa1 becomes hyper-phosphorylated by Cdc5 in kin4∆ cells (Figure 6E) (Maekawa et al., 2007; Pereira and Schiebel, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6E and citations to Maekawa et al., 2007; Pereira and Schiebel, 2005.

claim: Levels of the hyper-phosphorylated forms of Bfa1 were strongly reduced in spc72∆ cells.
source: Levels of the hyper-phosphorylated forms of Bfa1 were strongly reduced in spc72∆ cells (Figure 6E), although Kin4 was not able to phosphorylate Bfa1 in these cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Not only Kin4 but also Cdc5 requires Spc72 to efficiently phosphorylate Bfa1.
source: Thus, not only Kin4 but also Cdc5 requires Spc72 to efficiently phosphorylate Bfa1.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing reduced Bfa1 hyper-phosphorylation in spc72∆ cells.

claim: Spc72 serves as a platform that integrates Kin4 and Cdc5 counteracting actions on Bfa1.
source: Our data altogether suggests that Spc72 serves as a platform that integrates Kin4 and Cdc5 counteracting actions on Bfa1.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the data showing that both Kin4 and Cdc5 require Spc72 to phosphorylate Bfa1.

claim: Spc72-GBP constitutively recruited Bfa1-GFP to both SPBs regardless of the spindle position.
source: Spc72-GBP constitutively recruited Bfa1-GFP to both SPBs regardless of the spindle position (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Coexistence of Bfa1-GFP and Spc72-GBP in the same cell resulted in SPOC failure.
source: Emphasizing the importance of Spc72-Bfa1 disengagement for SPOC, coexistence of Bfa1-GFP and Spc72-GBP in the same cell resulted in SPOC failure (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: In the presence of Spc72-GBP, Bfa1-GFP accumulated hyper-phosphorylated forms, which disappeared upon depletion of Cdc5.
source: In the presence of Spc72-GBP, Bfa1-GFP accumulated hyper-phosphorylated forms, which disappeared upon depletion of Cdc5 (Figure 7C, lanes 3 ,4 and 5).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Persistence of Spc72-Bfa1 interaction provokes Cdc5 dependent phosphorylation of Bfa1.
source: Thus, persistence of Spc72-Bfa1 interaction provokes Cdc5 dependent phosphorylation of Bfa1.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing increased Cdc5-dependent phosphorylation of Bfa1 when Bfa1 is tethered to Spc72.

claim: Kin4 contributed to the phosphorylation of Bfa1-GFP in Spc72-GBP cells.
source: Importantly, Kin4 also contributed to the phosphorylation of Bfa1-GFP in Spc72-GBP cells, as deletion of KIN4 reduced the hyper-phosphorylated forms of Bfa1 (Figure 7C, lanes 4 and 6).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Bfa1 dissociates from Spc72 to prevent the inhibitory phosphorylation of Bfa1 by Cdc5.
source: Our data suggests a model where Bfa1 dissociates from Spc72 to prevent the inhibitory phosphorylation of Bfa1 by Cdc5 (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the data showing that forced Bfa1-Spc72 interaction leads to increased Cdc5 phosphorylation and SPOC failure.

claim: SPOC deficient phenotypes (multiple spindles and/or buds) accumulate with a high frequency (> 40%) in spc72∆ cultures.
source: However, in contrast to kar9∆ cells, SPOC deficient phenotypes (multiple spindles and/or buds) accumulate with a high frequency (> 40%) in spc72∆ cultures (Figure 8A) (Hoepfner et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8A and a citation to Hoepfner et al., 2002.

claim: In a kar9∆ population most of the cells reoriented their spindle in less than 50 min after anaphase onset.
source: In a kar9∆ population most of the cells reoriented their spindle in less than 50 min after anaphase onset.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Spindle mis-orientation persisted for longer than 50 min in the majority of spc72∆ cells.
source: In contrast, spindle mis-orientation persisted for longer than 50 min in the majority of spc72∆ cells (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The spindles of spc72∆ cells that remained arrested in anaphase for an extended period (> 50 min) broke down as a consequence of mitotic exit.
source: The spindles of spc72∆ cells that remained arrested in anaphase for an extended period (> 50 min) broke down as a consequence of mitotic exit (Figure 8C and 6D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8C and 6D.

claim: spc72∆ cells that underwent prolonged arrest re-entered the cell cycle to become binucleate cells.
source: These cells re-entered the cell cycle to become binucleate cells (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The SPOC was unable to maintain an indefinite cell cycle arrest in spc72∆ cells with prolonged spindle misalignment.
source: This indicated that the SPOC was unable to maintain an indefinite cell cycle arrest in this population of cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of SPOC slippage in spc72∆ cells after prolonged arrest.

claim: In the majority of binucleated spc72∆ cells that entered anaphase (10 out of 15 cells), one spindle remained in the mother cell compartment while the second entered the bud.
source: Interestingly, in the majority of binucleated cells that entered anaphase (10 out of 15 cells), one spindle remained in the mother cell compartment while the second entered the bud (Figure 8D, upper panel).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: In binucleated spc72∆ cells with one correctly aligned and one misaligned spindle, both spindles disassembled simultaneously as the cells exited mitosis.
source: In all such cells, the mother-bud oriented spindle and the misoriented spindle disassembled simultaneously, as the cells exited mitosis (Figure 8D and E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8D and E.

claim: Binucleated spc72∆ cells harboring two mis-oriented spindles remained arrested in late anaphase with intact anaphase spindles.
source: This behavior was not due to binucleation per se, because cells harboring two mis-oriented spindles remained arrested in late anaphase with intact anaphase spindles (Figure 8D, lower panel, and Figure 8E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8D and E.

claim: Satisfaction of the SPOC by the correctly aligned spindle triggers a dominant signal that silences or bypasses the SPOC throughout the cell.
source: This indicates that satisfaction of the SPOC by the correctly aligned spindle triggers a dominant signal that silences or bypasses the SPOC throughout the cell.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that one correctly aligned spindle is sufficient to trigger mitotic exit in binucleated cells with one misaligned spindle.

claim: The dominant mitotic exit signal is likely to be a diffusible signal.
source: This signal is likely to be a diffusible signal as the breakdown of the correctly aligned and misaligned nuclei occurs simultaneously.
evidence: This is inferred from the simultaneous breakdown of both spindles.

claim: Inefficiency of spindle re-orientation, together with SPOC leakage after prolonged arrest, leads to the accumulation of binucleated cells in spc72∆ cells.
source: In conclusion, inefficiency of spindle re-orientation, together with SPOC leakage after prolonged arrest, leads to the accumulation of binucleated cells in spc72∆ cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing prolonged spindle misalignment and SPOC slippage in spc72∆ cells.

claim: Binucleated spc72∆ cells have a higher probability of producing bi- or multinucleated cells in the next round of cell division, as one correctly aligned spindle is sufficient to disable SPOC signaling for both itself and its misaligned neighbor.
source: Binucleated cells, on the other hand, have a higher probability of producing bi- or multinucleated cells in the next round of cell division, as one correctly aligned spindle is sufficient to disable SPOC signaling for both itself and its misaligned neighbor.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that one correctly aligned spindle triggers mitotic exit in binucleated cells.

claim: spc72∆ populations accumulate bi- and multiple-nuclei even though they are SPOC proficient.
source: Altogether these data explain why spc72∆ populations accumulate bi- and multiple-nuclei even though they are SPOC proficient.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing SPOC slippage and dominant mitotic exit signal in binucleated cells.

claim: Direct physical interaction between Nud1 and Bfa1 has been previously demonstrated using recombinant proteins.
source: Recombinant proteins have previously been used to demonstrate the direct physical interaction between Nud1 and Bfa1 (Gruneberg et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gruneberg et al., 2000.

claim: Full length GST-Spc72 bound to MBP-Bfa1 but not to MBP-beads.
source: Full length GST-Spc72 bound to MBP-Bfa1 but not to MBP-beads (Figure 1B, lanes 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro binding data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The C-terminal 391 amino acids of Spc72 were sufficient to confer interaction with Bfa1.
source: The C-terminal 391 amino acids of Spc72 were sufficient to confer this interaction, as 6His-Spc72-C associated with MBP-Bfa1 but not to MBP (Figure 1B, lanes 3 and 4).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro binding data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: MBP-Bfa1 or MBP did not interact with an unrelated 6His-tagged protein (6His-Mlc1).
source: Notably, MBP-Bfa1 or MBP did not interact with an unrelated 6His-tagged protein (6His-Mlc1) to highlight the specific nature of the association with 6His-Spc72-C (Figure 1B, lanes 5 and 6).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro binding data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Bfa1 directly binds to Nud1 and Spc72 in vitro.
source: Taken together, Bfa1 directly binds to Nud1 and Spc72 in vitro, suggesting that the interactions established by FRET arise from direct physical interactions.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro binding data and previous literature.

claim: A positive FRET between two fluorophores only occurs when the fluorophores are in close apposition (< 10 nm).
source: A positive FRET between two fluorophores only occurs when the fluorophores are in close apposition (< 10 nm). This indicates that the fluorophore-fused proteins are in close proximity and likely to physically interact (Zal and Gascoigne, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zal and Gascoigne, 2004.

claim: Acceptor photobleaching FRET yielded more robust measurements for Bfa1-Bub2 SPB interactions compared to sensitized emission FRET.
source: In comparison to sensitized emission FRET, acceptor photobleaching FRET yielded more robust measurements for Bfa1-Bub2 SPB interactions.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison of the two FRET methods.

claim: FRET interactions between Bfa1-Nud1 and Bfa1-Spc72 most likely reflect physical interactions at SPBs in vivo.
source: Thus, FRET interactions between Bfa1-Nud1 and Bfa1-Spc72 most likely reflect physical interactions at SPBs in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the FRET data and in vitro binding data.

claim: C-terminally tagged Bfa1 yielded positive FRET with N-terminally tagged Bub2 at SPBs.
source: C-terminally tagged Bfa1 also yielded positive FRET with N-terminally tagged Bub2 at SPBs, which is in agreement with the fact that Bfa1 and Bub2 bind to SPBs as a bipartite complex (Caydasi and Pereira, 2009; Pereira et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by FRET data and citations to Caydasi and Pereira, 2009; Pereira et al., 2000.

claim: Bfa1 and Bub2 bind to SPBs as a bipartite complex.
source: C-terminally tagged Bfa1 also yielded positive FRET with N-terminally tagged Bub2 at SPBs, which is in agreement with the fact that Bfa1 and Bub2 bind to SPBs as a bipartite complex (Caydasi and Pereira, 2009; Pereira et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Caydasi and Pereira, 2009; Pereira et al., 2000.

claim: The remodeling of Bfa1-SPB binding is triggered by Kin4 phosphorylation of Bfa1.
source: We propose that the remodeling of Bfa1-SPB binding is triggered by Kin4 phosphorylation of Bfa1.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data showing that Kin4 is required for loss of Bfa1-Spc72 FRET.

claim: As a direct consequence of Kin4 phosphorylation, Bmh1 binds to Bfa1 and breaks Bfa1-Spc72 proximity.
source: As a direct consequence of this phosphorylation, Bmh1 binds to Bfa1 and breaks Bfa1-Spc72 proximity (Figure 7D) (Caydasi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data and supported by a citation to Caydasi et al., 2014.

claim: The reorganization of Bfa1-SPB binding may result from a possible Bfa1 conformational change triggered by recruitment of Bmh1 to Kin4 phosphorylated Bfa1.
source: The reorganization of Bfa1-SPB binding may result from a possible Bfa1 conformational change triggered by recruitment of Bmh1 to Kin4 phosphorylated Bfa1.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed by the authors.

claim: Such regulation may resemble the conformational change that Mad2 undergoes upon activation of the spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC).
source: Such regulation may resemble the conformational change that Mad2 undergoes upon activation of the spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC) (Luo et al., 2002; 2004; Mapelli et al., 2007; Mapelli and Musacchio, 2007; Sironi et al., 2002; Yang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a speculative comparison supported by citations to SAC literature.

claim: Spc72 has been proposed to constitute a part of the SPOC mechanism that senses cytoplasmic microtubule failure and recruits Kin4 to SPBs in response to this defect.
source: Spc72 has been proposed to constitute a part of the SPOC mechanism that senses cytoplasmic microtubule failure and recruits Kin4 to SPBs in response to this defect (Maekawa et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Maekawa et al., 2007.

claim: Cdc5 interacts with Spc72.
source: Given that Cdc5 interacts with Spc72 and phosphorylates Bfa1 at the SPB (Archambault and Glover, 2008; Maekawa et al., 2007; Park et al., 2004; Snead et al., 2007), it is tempting to speculate that Cdc5 only phosphorylates Bfa1 when in complex with Spc72.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Archambault and Glover, 2008; Maekawa et al., 2007; Park et al., 2004; Snead et al., 2007.

claim: Cdc5 phosphorylates Bfa1 at the SPB.
source: Given that Cdc5 interacts with Spc72 and phosphorylates Bfa1 at the SPB (Archambault and Glover, 2008; Maekawa et al., 2007; Park et al., 2004; Snead et al., 2007), it is tempting to speculate that Cdc5 only phosphorylates Bfa1 when in complex with Spc72.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Archambault and Glover, 2008; Maekawa et al., 2007; Park et al., 2004; Snead et al., 2007.

claim: Cdc5 only phosphorylates Bfa1 when in complex with Spc72.
source: Given that Cdc5 interacts with Spc72 and phosphorylates Bfa1 at the SPB (Archambault and Glover, 2008; Maekawa et al., 2007; Park et al., 2004; Snead et al., 2007), it is tempting to speculate that Cdc5 only phosphorylates Bfa1 when in complex with Spc72.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed by the authors.

claim: Disruption of the Bfa1-Spc72 interaction in cells with mis-oriented spindles might be a way to insulate the GAP complex from being inhibited by Cdc5.
source: In this case, disruption of the Bfa1-Spc72 interaction in cells with mis-oriented spindles might be a way to insulate the GAP complex from being inhibited by Cdc5 (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data.

claim: Bfa1-Spc72 tethering caused increased phosphorylation of Bfa1 by Cdc5 and hence SPOC failure.
source: In support of our model, Bfa1-Spc72 tethering caused increased phosphorylation of Bfa1 by Cdc5 and hence SPOC failure.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: Phosphorylation of Bfa1 by Kin4 was observed in Spc72-GBP cells.
source: Interestingly, phosphorylation of Bfa1 by Kin4 was also observed in these cells.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Kin4 can only inhibit Bfa1 phosphorylation by Cdc5 if Bfa1 dissociates from Spc72.
source: This indicates that Kin4 can only inhibit Bfa1 phosphorylation by Cdc5 if Bfa1 dissociates from Spc72.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing that Kin4 phosphorylates Bfa1 in Spc72-GBP cells but cannot prevent Cdc5 phosphorylation.

claim: Bfa1 phosphorylated by Kin4 is still a substrate of Cdc5 in vitro.
source: This is in line with the observation that Bfa1 phosphorylated by Kin4 is still a substrate of Cdc5 in vitro (Maekawa et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Maekawa et al., 2007.

claim: The binding affinity of Bfa1 to Nud1 must be higher than to Spc72.
source: If this is the case, the binding affinity of Bfa1 to Nud1 must be higher than to Spc72.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Bfa1 binds to SPBs via Nud1 in the absence of Spc72.

claim: The old SPB binds more Spc72 molecules then the new one.
source: Recently, it was shown that the old SPB binds more Spc72 molecules then the new one (Juanes et al., 2013), raising the possibility that Spc72 could be the determinant of Bfa1 SPB binding asymmetry.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Juanes et al., 2013.

claim: Bfa1 asymmetry is maintained even when Spc72 is absent through stable binding to Nud1.
source: However, our data indicate that Bfa1 asymmetry is maintained even when Spc72 is absent through stable binding to Nud1.
evidence: This is supported by data showing Bfa1 asymmetry in spc72∆ cells.

claim: Randomization of SPB inheritance did not alter the asymmetric association of Bfa1 with the dSPB.
source: In addition, randomization of SPB inheritance (through transient microtubule depolymerization) did not alter the asymmetric association of Bfa1 with the dSPB (Juanes et al., 2013; Pereira et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Juanes et al., 2013; Pereira et al., 2001.

claim: In cells with normal aligned spindles, Bfa1 is still in close proximity to Spc72 and Nud1 at both SPBs.
source: Furthermore, our FRET analyses show that, in cells with normal aligned spindles, Bfa1 is still in close proximity to Spc72 and Nud1 at both SPBs.
evidence: This is supported by FRET data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: It is unlikely that the asymmetric SPB binding of Bfa1-Bub2 arises from association of Bfa1 with different receptors at mother and daughter SPBs.
source: We thus consider it as unlikely that the asymmetric SPB binding of Bfa1-Bub2 arises from association of Bfa1 with different receptors at mother and daughter SPBs.
evidence: This is inferred from the FRET data showing similar FRET at both SPBs.

claim: Bub2 is subjected to phospho-regulation.
source: The asymmetry of Bfa1 at SPBs could arise from differential phospho-regulation at the poles. This regulation could be at the level of Bfa1, Nud1 or Bub2, which is also required for Bfa1 SPB asymmetry and subjected to phospho-regulation (Hu and Elledge, 2002; Maekawa et al., 2007; Park et al., 2008; Rock et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hu and Elledge, 2002; Maekawa et al., 2007; Park et al., 2008; Rock et al., 2013.

claim: Cdc5 has been previously suggested to preferentially target Bfa1 to the dSPB.
source: Cdc5 has been previously suggested to preferentially target Bfa1 to the dSPB (Kim et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kim et al., 2012.

claim: Bfa1 asymmetry was not disturbed in Cdc5-depleted cells.
source: However, the fact that Bfa1 asymmetry was not disturbed in Cdc5-depleted cells challenges this view (Caydasi and Pereira, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Caydasi and Pereira, 2009.

claim: Kin4 does not contribute to the reduced levels of Bfa1 at the mSPB.
source: Existing data indicated that Kin4 does not contribute to the reduced levels of Bfa1 at the mSPB (Caydasi and Pereira, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Caydasi and Pereira, 2009.

claim: Bfa1 asymmetry is not disturbed in spc72∆ cells, where Cdc5 and Kin4 do not phosphorylate Bfa1.
source: In addition, our data now shows that Bfa1 asymmetry is not disturbed in spc72∆ cells, where Cdc5 and Kin4 do not phosphorylate Bfa1.
evidence: This is supported by data showing Bfa1 asymmetry in spc72∆ cells.

claim: Kinases other than Kin4 and Cdc5 are involved in Bfa1 asymmetry, if the regulation is at the level of phosphorylation.
source: These observations suggest that kinases other than Kin4 and Cdc5 are involved in Bfa1 asymmetry, if the regulation is at the level of phosphorylation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Bfa1 asymmetry is maintained in the absence of Kin4 and Cdc5 phosphorylation.

claim: It has been proposed that Bfa1-Bub2 asymmetry is established through cytoplasmic microtubule-cortex interactions.
source: It has been proposed that Bfa1-Bub2 asymmetry is established through cytoplasmic microtubule-cortex interactions (Caydasi and Pereira, 2009; Monje-Casas and Amon, 2009; Pereira et al., 2001) or cell polarity determinants (Monje-Casas and Amon, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Caydasi and Pereira, 2009; Monje-Casas and Amon, 2009; Pereira et al., 2001.

claim: Bfa1 asymmetry was maintained in spc72∆ cells, which have very short and unstable cytoplasmic microtubules.
source: Bfa1 asymmetry was maintained in spc72∆ cells, which have very short and unstable cytoplasmic microtubules (Hoepfner et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by data and a citation to Hoepfner et al., 2002.

claim: Cells do not require an intact cytoplasmic microtubule cytoskeleton to establish and/or maintain Bfa1-Bub2 asymmetry.
source: This implies that cells do not require an intact cytoplasmic microtubule cytoskeleton to establish and/or maintain Bfa1-Bub2 asymmetry.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Bfa1 asymmetry is maintained in spc72∆ cells with defective cytoplasmic microtubules.

claim: SPOC is not an everlasting checkpoint.
source: Our data show that SPOC is not an everlasting checkpoint.
evidence: This is supported by data showing SPOC slippage after prolonged arrest.

claim: Slippage from SPOC can occur after prolonged mitotic arrest.
source: Slippage from SPOC can occur after prolonged mitotic arrest.
evidence: This is supported by data showing SPOC slippage in spc72∆ cells.

claim: In kar9∆ cells, SPOC slippage is a relatively rare event because the spindle is able to realign quickly in the majority of the cells due to the presence of the alternative dynein-dependent spindle alignment pathway.
source: In kar9∆ cells, this is a relatively rare event because the spindle is able to realign quickly in the majority of the cells due to the presence of the alternative dynein-dependent spindle alignment pathway (Eshel et al., 1993; Li et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by data and citations to Eshel et al., 1993; Li et al., 1993.

claim: Lack of functional cytoplasmic microtubules impairs spindle realignment in the majority of the spc72∆ cells.
source: Lack of functional cytoplasmic microtubules impairs spindle realignment in the majority of the spc72∆ cells.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: A similar phenomenon of dominant mitotic exit signal was described in binucleated budding yeast cells obtained by other means.
source: A similar phenomenon was described in binucleated budding yeast cells obtained by other means (Falk et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Falk et al., 2016.

claim: Lte1 is a putative Tem1 guanine nucleotide exchange factor.
source: Daughter cell specific factors, such as the putative Tem1 guanine nucleotide exchange factor Lte1 (Adames et al., 2001; Bardin et al., 2000; Keng et al., 1994; Pereira et al., 2000; Shirayama et al., 1994) could trigger the MEN to initiate mitotic exit in the bud.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Adames et al., 2001; Bardin et al., 2000; Keng et al., 1994; Pereira et al., 2000; Shirayama et al., 1994.

claim: Active GTP-bound Tem1 would fully activate the phosphatase Cdc14 that in turn counteracts and decreases the activity of mitotic cyclin-dependent kinase (Cdk) to promote mitotic exit and cytokinesis.
source: Active GTP-bound Tem1 would then fully activate the phosphatase Cdc14 that in turn counteracts and decreases the activity of mitotic cyclin-dependent kinase (Cdk) to promote mitotic exit and cytokinesis (Bardin and Amon, 2001; Meitinger et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bardin and Amon, 2001; Meitinger et al., 2012.

claim: Lte1 is a Kin4 inhibitor.
source: Interestingly, Lte1 is also a Kin4 inhibitor (Bertazzi et al., 2011; Falk et al., 2011), implying that bud specific factors may promote MEN activation through inhibition of SPOC components (SPOC silencing).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bertazzi et al., 2011; Falk et al., 2011.

claim: Cdc5 was proposed to inhibit Bfa1-Bub2 GAP activity in cells with normal aligned spindle.
source: Cdc5 was proposed to inhibit Bfa1-Bub2 GAP activity in cells with normal aligned spindle (Geymonat et al., 2002; 2003; Hu and Elledge, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Geymonat et al., 2002; 2003; Hu and Elledge, 2002.

claim: Factors other than Cdc5 inactivate Bfa1-Bub2 in the daughter cell compartment.
source: However, it is likely that factors other than Cdc5 inactivate Bfa1-Bub2 in the daughter cell compartment.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that spc72∆ cells exit mitosis normally despite reduced Cdc5 phosphorylation of Bfa1.

claim: Bfa1-Bub2 was not efficiently phosphorylated by Cdc5 in spc72∆ cells, yet these cells did not have a delayed mitotic exit when their mitotic spindle was correctly aligned.
source: We found that Bfa1-Bub2 was not efficiently phosphorylated by Cdc5 in spc72∆ cells, yet these cells did not have a delayed mitotic exit when their mitotic spindle was correctly aligned.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6E and 6D.

claim: A mutant form of Bfa1 (Bfa1-11A), which cannot be phosphorylated by Cdc5, does not cause a delayed mitotic exit.
